title: Anybody Headed Down Today?
intro: Priya's on the register at Middle Brook in Jefferson, and half her kid's costume needs to be in the city tonight. Walt's the one who drives down — he's up at J&H with the truck.
smallTalk: Priya's kid has a showcase in the city tonight. Half the village knows and it isn't even nine.
Walt's truck is sitting on J&H's lot with the hood up. He'll be taking it personally.
Best place in the county to break down, if you have to, is a forecourt with the coffee on.
Somebody told me to ask a Jess. I'd have liked to know which one.
The trail's dry the whole way to Hobart this week. Somebody's already walked it this morning.
Tops finally got the good peaches in.
This has been the soggiest summer anybody up here can remember, and everybody's got an opinion about it.
Word travels faster than traffic on Route 10, and that's saying something.
Nice to see everybody pitching in for Priya's kid.
Somebody's fixing up the space under Stamford Coffee. Ask ten people what it's going to be and you'll get eleven answers.
Stamford Coffee's got a record on and a whole shelf of coffee makers lined up like a parade. Go look, it's worth the trip on its own.
If you're late getting home, the self-serve fridge at Stamford Coffee has dinner in it. That fridge has saved a lot of Tuesdays.
80 Main's got the Catskills sweaters in again. I'm not saying I need another one. I'm saying I'm going to look.

items.name: Priya's costume bag
items.blurb: Half a dance costume, sequins and all.

items.name: Jess R.'s jumper cables
items.blurb: Red and black, coiled neat. They live behind the seat of her truck.

lines: He texted a photo from the stage door the second it got there — you'll just have to imagine it, but trust me, it's a whole look.
Thank you, truly. And thank whoever else you ended up standing in a lot with this morning.
Cables! Then you're most of the way there.
Tell Walt I said thank you before he starts telling you about the truck, or you'll not get another word in.
His truck won't start? Poor Walt. He'll be more bothered about the truck than about my bag, I promise you.
Walt's up at J&H, the gas station on the corner, with the truck. Start there and I expect you'll finish there.
My kid's in a dance showcase in the city tonight, and half his costume is still sitting on our kitchen table. It's in this bag.

I'm on the register here at Middle Brook till four, and it's three hours down — he needs it in his hands by five, when they call them in. So it isn't me that's taking it. Here — would you carry it for me?
Ask Walt. He's up at J&H with the truck, and he goes down every other Sunday.
Caught first turn of the key once she'd had a proper drink. Bag's riding up front where I can see it, and I'm away as soon as I've drunk this coffee.
Tell the kid break a leg from me.
Cables. Good. Now we want a car alongside with something left in it, running a good ten minutes — she'll not take a quick touch and say thank you.
Find me a Jess with a car and nowhere to be, and we're in business.
Still here. Still dead. Still glad it happened on this lot and not halfway up the hill.
Ask a Jess. Two in Stamford, one down in Hobart, and one somewhere round this village who's never where I've just looked.
Priya's kid's costume? Course I'll take it. Every other Sunday, and today's a Sunday. Hand it over when I'm moving.
Only I'm not moving. Battery's dead as a stone, and my cables are hanging on a nail in the barn eight miles up the hill, which is exactly where they're no use to anybody.
Ask a Jess. There's four of 'em between here and Hobart and I have never once got the right one first go.
Morning. Hood's up, which tells you most of it — she turned over twice and then thought better of the whole idea.
No better place to be stuck, mind. J&H will let a man leave a truck on the lot all day and bring the coffee out to him while he thinks about it.
Walt's away, then. And you've met more of us in one morning than most people manage in a year.
You've got Jess R.'s cables, I see — she'd lend them to anyone. Now find somebody with a car and no particular hurry. That's the harder half.
The trail, I said — the south end, where the old rail bed starts. She'll be the one with the pack on.
Walt's truck? It's a good truck having a bad morning.
Jess R. went past me at eight with a pack on, headed for the trail — and that woman has never once been without a set of cables behind her seat.
Morning! Lovely day for standing around on Main Street, which is what I'm doing, and I'd recommend it.
Truck's away? Good. I'll get the cables back off Walt eventually — I always do, and they always come back with a story attached.
Go on, then. I've got eleven miles of old rail bed to be getting on with and it won't walk itself.
Cables? Behind the seat of my truck, where they live. Hang on.
There you go. Leave them with Walt when you're done — he's good for them, and I'm headed the other way.

effects.toast: You've got Jess R.'s jumper cables.

lines: Eleven miles of old rail bed to Hobart and not one hill worth the name. I'll be there by lunch.
If you've never walked it, walk it. You can hear the creek most of the way.
She's away, then. Ten minutes, like I said. There's nothing wrong with that truck a bit of patience doesn't fix.
Walt's away, then. Ten minutes of a car alongside and that truck's fine. It always was.
Cables in hand — that's half of it. Now the car, and somebody content to sit in it a while.
Cables, a car, and ten patient minutes. That's the whole recipe.
Walt's green pickup? I've had my head under that hood. She's not a quick-jump sort — you can touch cables to that battery all day and get nothing back.
What she wants is a car pulled up alongside her, running, for a good ten minutes. Somebody content to sit a while with the radio on.
This is the best spot in Hobart. You can hear the creek underneath everything else.
Ten minutes and she was fine. A good excuse to sit and do nothing, honestly. I'd have given it twenty.
Cables in your hand, Walt's truck twenty feet that way, and me sitting here with a full tank and nowhere I have to be all morning.
Well, come on then. It'd be rude not to.
Walt's stuck? I'd pull round this minute, only a car alongside does nothing at all on its own.
And my cables went off in the trunk of the car I sold in April, which was careless of me and I have heard about it since.
That's my wagon down at the end of the lot there. I'm not sitting in it because it's a nicer morning out here than in.
No, I'm not waiting on anything. That's the best part of it.
Tell me that bag made it to the stage door in one piece.
Cables in hand. Now you want somebody with a car and a bit of patience, and this county is full of both.
Walt's truck won't go? Then it's a Jess he wants.
Somebody was in here this morning saying a Jess was going up to sort him out. Nobody asked me which.
Walt's your man, up at J&H in Jefferson. Every other Sunday, regular as the mail.
Morning! Coffee's on, and the sundae bar's real, if you're curious.
Priya's asking up in Jefferson about getting something down to the city tonight. She's on the register at Middle Brook till four.
Glad it worked out. Come by Cellar Door for a tasting sometime, once things settle down.
Cables from Jess R.? Then you're nearly there. A car and ten minutes, and that's the lot.
Walt's off the road too? My truck's been in the shop two weeks. The two of us could start a club, and it would have to meet on foot.
Jess T. had her own hood up half of last winter and never once called anyone. She's over by the bridge most mornings, watching the water go past.
Priya's costume run? Word travels. Not me today — my truck's still in the shop.
Walt goes down every other Sunday. He's the one to ask.
Welcome — pull up a seat on the bench anytime.
If you're headed up toward Jefferson, say hello to Priya at Middle Brook. I hear she's asking around about something.
So Walt got away after all. Every other Sunday, like clockwork, give or take a battery. Tell Priya's kid break a leg from all of us in here.
Somebody came in saying Walt's stuck on the lot at J&H with the hood up. He'll be fine — nobody's stuck long around here, they just end up with a great deal of advice.
Still a gallery downstairs, by the way. I've not been talked out of it.
Still a gallery downstairs, whatever you've been told. I've not been talked out of it.
They put paper over the window before I could get a look. I respect that. I'm still going to try.
Sit anywhere — you can hear the record player from every table in here, so you get whichever side they've put on.
Have you heard? Somebody's doing something with the space underneath us. Hammering all last week. Nobody knows what it is, including the counter, and the counter knows everything.
My money's on a gallery. Half the people at these tables paint. I've seen the sketchbooks.
Nothing new downstairs? Everyone's still guessing. Oysters — that's my guess and I'm not moving. The wine nights in here fill right up; imagine that every night of the week.
Whoever it is, they've picked a lovely spot. Coffee upstairs, sweaters next door. I'd open there.
Don't mind me, I'm deciding between two sweaters and losing.
You've noticed the work going on under the coffee shop? Whole town's noticed. Nobody's got the answer, which hasn't slowed anybody down.
My guess is an oyster bar. The oyster-and-wine nights in here fill right up — somebody's clearly been paying attention.
Still no answer on the space under the coffee shop. Dog treats, I'm telling you. Look at this deck — every dog in Stamford naps here. That's a customer base.
Biscuit here has been sniffing at that papered-over window every walk this week. He knows something. He's not telling either.
Morning. Biscuit likes to check the patio before we go anywhere else, so we check the patio.
Have you heard about the space underneath the coffee shop? Somebody's doing it up. There's paper on the window and hammering behind it, and that's all anybody knows.
My guess is dog treats. Every dog in Stamford naps on this deck. Somebody's finally noticed.
Right alongside you, Walt. Red to red, black on the bracket, and then we let her have a drink a while.
I'm in no rush. I'd have sat on that wall another hour quite happily.
...There she is. Listen to that.
Jess L. Course it was. There's five of us if you count me, you know — Jess is my own middle name, my grandmother's doing.
Bag on the passenger seat where I can see it — stage door by six.
And I still never get the right one first go.

steps.toast: Episode complete — new story next week

lines: Taped inside the door, in careful marker: "The truck on the lot is Walt's. He knows. He's on it." Somebody has drawn a small encouraging sun beside it.
Pinned to the board by the door: somebody's asking if anybody's headed down to the city tonight. Two people have already written "ask Walt" underneath, in two different pens.
Down the side of the coffee shop, a low window right at the ground, with brown paper and a sheet of plywood over it from the inside. Somebody's at work behind it — you can hear a saw going.
Not a word written on any of it. Everybody who walks past leans in for a look anyway, and comes away knowing exactly as much as before.
